title: A 13,800-year-old base camp in interior Alaska shows early Americans settling in for the long haul
dek: At Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ, archaeologists found a hearth, a possible dwelling, the hemisphere's oldest needles, and wolf-like canids that may have lived alongside people.
body: Fifty-five kilometres southeast of Fairbanks, a site whose name means "They were there" in an Athabascan language has yielded a hearth, a small pit, and the stain of a wooden post that researchers say could mark a sloping-roof shelter or early tent. If the interpretation holds, it would be one of the earliest constructed dwellings known in North America.

The team, led by Kelly Graf of the University of Kansas, dates the earliest occupation to roughly 13,800 years ago. That places the camp in eastern Beringia, the Ice Age land bridge connecting Siberia and Alaska, during the Late Pleistocene, when sea levels were low and the corridor between continents stood open.

Unlike the small, short-term hunting camps that dominate the early Beringian record, Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ produced tens of thousands of artefacts and animal remains across more than a thousand years of intermittent use. The density and variety of material, stone tools, bone needles, an earth oven packed with charcoal and bone, led researchers to classify it as a base camp where people carried out a wide range of daily tasks.

Among the stone tools are distinctive diamond-shaped bifaces made from rhyolite and basalt. Their technology matches artefacts from sites farther west in Beringia, including northern Siberia. Obsidian traced to sources hundreds of kilometres to the northwest shows raw material moving across vast distances, suggesting cultural connections linking Asian and North American Beringian communities.

The site also yielded the oldest known eyed needles in the Western Hemisphere. Bone needles like these would have allowed fitted, sewn clothing, essential for surviving Pleistocene Alaska. Similar needles appear later at sites farther south, hinting at a technological thread tying Beringian groups to populations beyond the ice sheets.

A perforated deer-antler pendant adds a personal ornament to the assemblage, a type documented at other early North American sites. Together, the needles, the pendant, and the stone-tool styles point to cultural links stretching both west into Siberia and south into the continent.

Perhaps the most arresting finds are the remains of more than a dozen wolf-like canids. One jawbone falls outside known dire wolf, Beringian wolf, and grey wolf populations, representing a distinct group in central Alaska. Earlier genetic work shows North America's first domestic dogs descended from Siberian wolves. The age and location of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ raise the possibility that some of these canids were associated with people, though the researchers stress the evidence is indirect and does not establish domestication.
doesnt_show: The canid remains do not demonstrate domestication or a direct dog-human relationship. The shelter interpretation is based on a post stain and pit, not a complete structure. Cultural connections inferred from tool similarities cannot confirm whether individuals travelled the full distances between Siberia and interior Alaska.
settle: Ancient DNA from the canid jaws and further excavation of the structural feature would clarify the nature of the human-canid association and confirm whether the post stain represents a dwelling.
